passages.happening:
Samson goes down to Timnah and sees a young Philistine woman (verse 1). He comes home and tells his parents, “I have seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah. Now get her for me as a wife” (verse 2).

His father and mother object. “Can’t you find a young woman among your relatives or among any of our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?” (verse 3). Samson answers his father, “Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes.”

Then the narrator adds a note in brackets. “Now his father and mother did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 announced a boy set apart for God. Chapter 14 shows the grown man, and the contrast is immediate. The first thing he wants is a woman of the people who rule over Israel, and he wants her because of how she looks.

Marriage was arranged by families. Samson's demand that his parents get her for him follows that custom, but his refusal to listen to them breaks it. His parents object because Israel's law forbade marriage with the peoples of the land, for fear that they would turn Israel's children to other gods. The Philistines did not share the sign of the covenant and worshiped other gods, so they fell within the spirit of that warning.

The Hebrew behind ‘pleasing to my eyes’ says, word for word, that she is right in his eyes. It looks ahead to the book's last verdict on the whole period, that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Samson is the book's picture of that in one man.

Timnah lay in the valley of Sorek, a few miles west of Samson's home, on the border between Israel and the Philistines. That Samson can go there freely and marry into a Philistine family shows how the two peoples lived side by side, the Philistines ruling but not always at war.

Then verse 4. The narrator does not say that God approved of Samson's desire. He says that God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines through it. The word for occasion is found with this meaning only here in the Hebrew Bible. Samson's parents could not see what God was doing. Neither, it seems, could Samson.
passages.later: Joseph said the same kind of thing about his brothers: “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). A proverb puts it simply: “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).
passages.hard:
How can Samson's choices be ‘from the LORD’ if they break God's law and come from selfish desire?

The narrator's words in verse 4 are careful. They do not say God approved of Samson's desire for a Philistine wife. They say God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines through it.

Scripture often says that God works through human wrongdoing without causing it or excusing it. Joseph told his brothers that they meant evil and God meant it for good. Christian teachers have called this God's providence: God governs all things, and people remain responsible for what they choose.

Readers differ on how far verse 4 goes. Some stress that it speaks of God's purpose and not of Samson's motives, and that Samson is fully to blame for what he does. Others think the verse suggests that God stirred Samson's attraction for his own ends. The chapter does not settle the question. It insists only that neither Samson's recklessness nor the power of the Philistines is outside God's control.
passages.asks: Samson chose what was right in his own eyes. Ask how much of what you want is decided by what pleases your eyes, and who in your life has the freedom to say no to you. And ask how you can trust that God is at work in a situation without pretending that the wrong in it is right.

passages.happening:
Samson goes down to Timnah with his father and mother. Among the vineyards of Timnah a young lion comes roaring at him (verse 5). Then “the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one would tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done” (verse 6). He goes on and talks with the woman, and he likes her (verse 7).

Some time later, on his way to marry her, he turns aside to look at the lion's carcass. Bees have made a hive in it, with honey (verse 8). He scoops out honey with his hands and eats it as he walks. He gives some to his parents, and they eat it, but he does not tell them where it came from (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The Spirit of the LORD ‘came powerfully upon him’. The Hebrew verb means to rush, a sudden, overwhelming force that gives strength for a task. The same verb is used later of the Spirit rushing on Saul and on David.

Then the carcass. Under the law, anyone who touched the carcass of an animal like a lion was unclean until evening. The Nazirite law in Numbers speaks of human dead bodies, not of animals, so it does not directly forbid this. But contact with death keeps coming back in Samson's story, and it raises the question of how seriously he took being set apart. He reaches into the carcass for honey, and he keeps it secret, even from his parents, who eat it without knowing.

Secrets run through this chapter. He does not tell his parents about the lion or the honey. The secret he keeps from his wife will become the one she gives away.
passages.later:
The law said of animals like the lion, “whoever touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening” (Leviticus 11:27). The law of the Nazirite, speaking of the human dead, said, “Throughout the days of his separation to the LORD, he must not go near a dead body” (Numbers 6:6).

The same rush of the Spirit came on Israel's first kings: “Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you” (1 Samuel 10:6), Samuel told Saul, and when David was anointed, “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13).
passages.asks: Samson had God's strength in his hands, and he used those same hands to break his vow in secret. Ask where you treat God's gifts as yours to use however you like. And ask what you are hiding from the people who love you, and whether the hiding has become a habit.

passages.t: The riddle at the wedding feast
passages.happening:
Samson's father goes to the woman's family, and Samson holds a feast there, as bridegrooms did (verse 10). The Philistines give him thirty young men as companions (verse 11).

Samson sets them a riddle. If they solve it within the seven days of the feast, he will give them thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes. If they cannot, they will give the same to him (verses 12-13). “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet” (verse 14).

For three days they cannot solve it. On the fourth they go to his wife: “Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father’s household to death” (verse 15). She weeps before Samson for the rest of the feast, and on the seventh day, worn down, he tells her. She tells her people (verses 16-17).

Before sunset on the seventh day the men answer, “What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?” (verse 18). Samson replies with a bitter insult.

“Then the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty of their men, took their apparel, and gave their clothes to those who had solved the riddle” (verse 19). He goes home burning with anger, and his wife is given to one of his companions (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
Wedding feasts lasted seven days. The Hebrew word for this feast comes from the verb to drink, which suggests a drinking party and raises the question of Samson's vow to drink no wine, though the text does not say whether he drank. The thirty companions were customary for a bridegroom, but here they also look like a guard. Riddles and wagers were common entertainment, and thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes were a large stake.

The riddle cannot be solved without knowing about the lion. The answer the men give is itself shaped like a riddle, and some scholars think it may have been a known riddle whose usual answer was love.

Look at what the men of the town do to Samson's wife. They threaten to burn her and her family alive. She is caught between her own people and her husband, and she gives way. The story does not blame her for the threat she lived under.

Samson's reply about plowing with his heifer is a crude and bitter image of his wife's part in it.

The Spirit rushes on him again, and he goes to Ashkelon, one of the five Philistine cities, more than twenty miles away, and kills thirty men there to pay his debt. The Spirit's gift is power for a task. It does not make Samson's anger holy, and the story does not pretend that it does. The chapter that began with a wedding ends in killing, a man going home in a rage, and a bride handed to another man.
passages.later:
Jacob's wedding, too, lasted a week: “Finish this week’s celebration” (Genesis 29:27).

The same Hebrew verb for enticing a person is used when the Philistine lords come to Delilah in chapter 16, and the two betrayals mirror each other.
passages.asks: The men of Timnah threatened Samson's wife, and she gave in. Ask whether you have ever pressed someone so hard that they had no good choice left. And ask what you do with your anger when you have been outwitted. Samson took his out on thirty strangers. Ask who pays for yours.
